---
title: "Before Lesson 1"
---

Install Sonic Pi 5.0.0 from [sonic-pi.net](https://sonic-pi.net/). The download
page covers macOS, Windows, Linux, and Raspberry Pi. This manuscript targets
that version so a changed synth default does not become an unexplained musical
difference.

Open Sonic Pi, paste this into an empty buffer, and press **Run**.

```{.ruby audio=""}
play 60
```

If you hear one note, the audio path works. If you do not, check the volume,
selected output device, and Sonic Pi log before changing the code.

Headphones or speakers with usable bass response help throughout the course.
Part 1 compares frequencies near 200 Hz, and Part 10 builds bass lines whose
shape can disappear through small laptop speakers. Keep the level low enough
that repeated drills remain comfortable.

## Which version

The examples are written for **Sonic Pi 5.0.0**. Their extracted Ruby has passed
syntax checks. The complete manuscript has not received a Sonic Pi runtime and
listening pass, so every lesson remains `draft`. There are no promised recordings
for untested examples; empty audio attributes mark the places where recordings
can be added after auditioning.

Sonic Pi can change synth defaults, samples, or function behaviour between
releases. If your version differs, check **Help, About** and record the difference
before adapting an example. A snippet that parses under Ruby may still call a
Sonic Pi function incorrectly or produce an unbalanced sound. The log and help
pane are the first diagnostic tools.

## The window

Three areas carry most of the work. **Buffers** hold code. Use a fresh one for
each example so definitions and live loops from an earlier lesson do not affect
the next. The **log** prints messages, notes, and errors. Read it whenever the
sound and the program disagree. The **help** pane documents synths, samples, and
functions for the installed version.

On macOS, `Cmd-R` runs the buffer and `Cmd-.` stops all sound. On Windows and
Linux, use `Alt-R` and `Alt-.`. Learn the stop command before running the first
live loop.

## A first sound

Paste the following program into a fresh buffer. It introduces several constructs
that Parts 0 through 3 unpack: tempo, synth selection, arrays, timed playback,
and concurrent loops.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

# E minor pentatonic keeps the first experiment focused on rhythm and timbre.
melody = [:e4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :d5, :b4, :a4, :g4]

live_loop :tune do
  melody.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.4
    sleep 0.25
  end
end

live_loop :bass do
  play :e2, release: 1.8, amp: 0.7, cutoff: 70
  sleep 2
end
```

Listen through two repetitions, then change one field. Replace `:pluck` with
`:prophet` and run the buffer again. The pitches and timing remain fixed while
the instrument changes. Restore `:pluck`, replace `melody` with
`[:e4, :f4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :c5, :d5, :e5]`, and compare again. Parts 2 and 5
explain why the second collection behaves differently over the E bass.

Press the stop shortcut before continuing. Live loops run until stopped, even
after you move to another buffer.

## How to use the draft

Work through lessons in order. Later helpers and representations assume earlier
ones, especially the event schema introduced before harmony and reused in
notation, transcription, and arrangement. Each lesson follows the same five
steps: hear the idea, run a complete program, change one input, connect the
result to theory, then attempt a finite extension.

Use the [solutions appendix](appendix/solutions.qmd) after making a real attempt.
Use the [glossary](appendix/glossary.qmd) to recover a term and the [Sonic Pi
cheat sheet](appendix/sonic-pi-cheatsheet.qmd) to recover a call. The [sources
ledger](appendix/sources.qmd) records the provenance needed for transcription
material.

When a lesson surprises you, write down the version, the exact edit, the log
output, and what you heard. A useful report distinguishes syntax failure, Sonic
Pi runtime failure, timing trouble, and disagreement with the prose. Those notes
are the evidence required to move a lesson from `draft` to `tested`.
